meta.title: The Charge Up the Hill
meta.skill_frame: Author's craft: read how the writer uses short sentences that speed the action and hold the reader in the moment.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured part_1 101w at FK 4.2, part_2 106w at FK 4.9, part_3 105w at FK 4.4. The load is short sentences and the narrator's close action; the language is deliberately simple.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.basis: Adapted from Theodore Roosevelt, The Rough Riders (1899), under DESIGN_RULES 2.5.
source.attribution: Theodore Roosevelt. The Rough Riders. 1899. Project Gutenberg eBook #13000, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/13000, accessed 2026-11-11. Public domain in the United States.
source.adaptation: The authoring pass split long sentences, dropped rare words, and simplified technical terms; no facts added.
source.survey: One paragraph of the Kettle Hill charge: the men cheering as they run, Roosevelt riding up the lane, the wire fence, and the last shots at the top.
source.drafted_by: LessonBot harness (DeepSeek 1017), adapted from the human source; source review completed

session.difficulty_basis: short sentences that speed the action and hold the reader in the moment

authoring_exceptions: part_1 measures FK 4.2 and part_3 FK 4.4, just below the 4-5 window; the short-sentence craft and the close action carry the load. Owner review required.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: By then we were all excited by the charge. The men cheered and ran forward between shots. The foremost officers' faces were delighted. Stevens of the Ninth ran at the head of his troops. Their faces will always stay in my mind. I galloped forward a few yards until I saw the men were well started. Then I galloped back to help Goodrich get his men across the road. He commanded his troop. They would attack the hill from that side. Captain Mills had already thrown three of the other troops of the regiment across this road for the same purpose.
passage.part_2: I wheeled around. I galloped toward the hill again. I passed the shouting, cheering, firing men. I went up the lane, splashing through a small stream. When I came level with the ranch buildings on top of Kettle Hill, I turned and went up the slope. I was on horseback, so I got ahead of the men on foot. My orderly, Henry Bardshar, was the exception. He had run ahead very fast to get better shots at the Spaniards. They were now running out of the ranch buildings. Sergeant Campbell and a number of the Arizona men, and Dudley Dean, among others, were very close behind.
passage.part_3: Stevens and his Ninth platoon were abreast of us. So were McNamee and Hartwick. Some forty yards from the top I ran into a wire fence and jumped off Little Texas, turning him loose. He had been scraped by a couple of bullets. One nicked my elbow. I never expected to see him again. I ran up the hill. Bardshar stopped to shoot. Two Spaniards fell as he emptied his magazine. These were the only Spaniards I actually saw fall to aimed shots by any one of my men, with the exception of two guerillas in trees. The men on foot were close behind us.

items.prompt: What had Captain Mills already done with three other troops of the regiment?

tutor_only.confirm: Captain Mills had already thrown three other troops across the road for the same purpose.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The answer is in the last sentence of part_1: 'Captain Mills had already thrown three of the other troops of the regiment across this road for the same purpose.'
tutor_only.tell: The last sentence of the opening gives this fact. It says Captain Mills had already sent three troops across the road.
help: Read the last sentence of the opening.
Find what Captain Mills had already done.
tutor_only.core_idea: Captain Mills had already sent three other troops across the road to attack the hill from that side.
accept_ideas: Captain Mills had already thrown three other troops across the road.
Captain Mills had already sent three troops across the road for the same purpose.
Three other troops of the regiment were already across the road to attack the hill from that side.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say Captain Mills commanded Goodrich's troop.

items.prompt: He rides forward, then turns back to help Goodrich's troop cross. What does turning back show about his responsibility?

tutor_only.confirm: He is responsible for getting other units into the attack, not only for his own ride.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The answer comes from 'I galloped forward a few yards until I saw the men were well started' and 'Then I galloped back to help Goodrich get his men across the road.'
tutor_only.tell: He checks that the charge is started, then turns back to get Goodrich's troop across the road. That is work beyond his own ride.
help: He first checks that the charge is moving. Then he goes back to help another troop cross.
tutor_only.core_idea: He is responsible for getting other units into the attack, not only for his own ride.
accept_ideas: He is responsible for more than his own charge.
He helps other units get into the attack.
He coordinates the attack, not only his own ride.
He makes sure Goodrich's troop crosses.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say he only wanted to help a friend.
if_they_say.ask: What does turning back show about what he is responsible for?

items.prompt: Bardshar ran ahead of the mounted narrator to get better shots at the Spaniards. What conclusion about the risk he took does this support but not state?

tutor_only.confirm: He moved closer to the enemy than the men behind him, so he took on greater danger.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The sentence says Bardshar ran ahead of the mounted narrator to get better shots at the Spaniards; moving closer to the enemy means he took on greater danger.
tutor_only.tell: Bardshar ran ahead alone, closer to the Spaniards than the narrator. Going closer to shoot means he took on more danger.
help: Look at where Bardshar was compared with the narrator and the men behind.
Closer to the enemy means more danger for the person who goes first.
tutor_only.core_idea: Bardshar moved ahead of the mounted narrator, nearer the enemy, to get better shots, so he took on greater danger than the men behind him.
accept_ideas: He took on greater danger by moving closer to the enemy.
He was more exposed than the men behind him.
He risked more to get a better shot.
He moved nearer the enemy than the narrator.
not_required: naming Kettle Hill or the ranch buildings
details about the Spaniards running out
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: He says Bardshar ran ahead because someone ordered him to.
if_they_say.ask: Does the passage say anyone ordered Bardshar forward?

tutor_only.full_idea: Bardshar moved ahead of the mounted narrator, nearer the enemy, to get better shots, so he took on greater danger than the men behind him.

items.prompt: Short sentences like 'I wheeled around. I galloped.' What does that rhythm do to the ride?

tutor_only.confirm: Each short sentence is one move, so the actions come one right after another.
tutor_only.correct_reason: 'I wheeled around. I galloped toward the hill again.' Each sentence is one action, so the moves follow with no pause between them.
tutor_only.tell: Each short sentence is one move. The actions come one right after another.
help: Find the short sentences that each name one move.
Notice that the next move starts as soon as the last one ends.
tutor_only.core_idea: Each sentence is one move, so the ride goes fast.
accept_ideas: Each sentence is one move, so the ride goes fast.
The actions come one right after another.
One move per sentence, with no pause between them.
The short sentences put each move in its own beat.
not_required: Saying the narrator is on horseback
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: They say the short sentences make the ride feel calm.
if_they_say.ask: What does each short sentence contain?

partial.when: The student says the ride feels exciting, urgent, or scary, without saying each sentence is one move.
partial.ask: What does each short sentence contain?

items.prompt: How does the writer's approach change from the opening to the last part?

tutor_only.confirm: The last part puts the writer in the close action on foot, in the fight himself.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Part_3 puts the narrator on foot in the close fight; the opening had him watching and directing the charge.
tutor_only.tell: The opening mostly shows the charge and troop movements. The last part puts the writer in the close action on foot.
help: Compare what the writer is doing in the opening with what he is doing in the last part.
Name the change in his role, not every event.
tutor_only.core_idea: The last part puts the writer in the close action on foot.
accept_ideas: He is in the close action on foot.
He is on foot in the close fight.
The writer puts himself in the close action.
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: The student says the writer only lists more events in part_3.
if_they_say.ask: What changes in the writer’s own role from the opening to the last part?
